newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Rosneft oil officials battle over sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Russian Rosneft oil officials battle over sell-off.

text.p: Deeply divided officials at Russia's Rosneft oil company met on Monday to try to settle major differences over how the last crown jewel in the Moscow government's energy portfolio should be privatised.

At the headquarters of the last big Russian oil company still to be entirely state-owned, board members battled behind closed doors over issues ranging from privatisation and stalled plans to issue a Eurobond to the recent resignations of senior executives and changes to the company's charter.
Officials in contact with the board told reporters waiting for news at Rosneft headquarters that members had voted to let board chairman Alexander Putilov handle the privatisation brief.
Putilov is locked in a bitter ideological debate with Rosneft president Yuri Bespalov over the company's future.
"Bespalov wants a strategic investor with maximum investment for the company," said Vladimir Vyunitsky, a new spokesman loyal to Bespalov and who is replacing spokesman Vladimir Tumarkin.
Tumarkin resigned with other top officials earlier this month over differences with Bespalov. But he is still carrying out some official duties.
Prime-Tass news agency quoted Putilov as saying over 50 percent of Rosneft would be sold at a special cash auction while three percent would remain in the hands of employees.
The remainder would be sold through an investment tender, where in addition to buying shares from the state, bidders must promise to plough new funds into the company.

Rosneft -- prized for its status at the state's agent in multi-billion dollar production-sharing deals with Western oil companies and its stake in a planned Kazakh-Russian oil pipeline -- is a test-case of how managers at Russia's top companies are battling each other to implement rival visions of the future.

Bespalov, an ex-industry minister and ally of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, wants to hand employees 10 percent of Rosneft, leave 51 percent with the state and sell the rest to a strategic investor.
Putilov, shifted from president to board chairman on orders from the Kremlin, wants the workers' collective to have a larger stake in the company.

The quarrels, over personalities as much as strategies, have paralysed development plans at vertically-integrated Rosneft, which was once envisioned as the national oil company but now handles under five percent of Russia's total crude oil output.
Company sources, speaking at Rosneft, said the battles had cast a cloud over Rosneft's plans to work with ABN-Amro and SBC Warburg to issue a Eurobond.
They said trade financing for deals on Russia's Far Eastern island of Sakhalin, where Rosneft is a shareholder in a major international oil project, was also jeopardised.

"It's Absurdistan," said outgoing spokesman Tumarkin, referring to the chill air at Rosneft, where some officials had been locked out of their offices and loyalties were split between those who supported the new leader, Bespalov, and those who backed his predecessor Putilov.
Foreign oil companies have been put off by the fact it is unclear with whom in Rosneft they must negotiate their stalled production-sharing contracts.

The battle for Rosneft involves Russia's top privatisation officials and reformers -- privatisation minister Alfred Kokh and Fuel and Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov -- both of whom are eager to sell chunks of the company to raise budget revenues.
It also involves Russian bankers and businessmen who are eyeing the company as a takeover target.
Boris Berezovsky, whose empire includes the Sibneft oil mini-major; Vladimir Potanin, president of Uneximbank; and domestic oil giant LUKoil are among those said to be eyeing Rosneft.
